material:
SITUATION: Stalking or sexual harassment of a woman. These offences are specifically covered, and the law has special rules to make reporting easier for women.
STEP 1: If you are in danger now, call 112. The Women Helpline numbers 181 and 1091 are also available in many states.
STEP 2: Keep evidence: screenshots, call logs, photos, the person's number, profile and any CCTV locations. Do not delete anything.
STEP 3: When a woman reports offences such as sexual harassment, stalking or outraging her modesty, the information must be recorded by a woman police officer. [BNSS 173(1), first proviso]
STEP 4: You can report at any police station, orally or electronically. It is read back to you, you sign it, and you get a copy free of cost. [BNSS 173(1)-(2)]
STEP 5: If the police refuse, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate. [BNSS 173(4)]
STEP 6: If you fear for your safety as a witness, ask about the witness protection scheme. [BNSS 398]
KEEP READY: Messages, call logs, screenshots; Dates and places of each incident; Witnesses or CCTV; A trusted person who can accompany you to the police station
SECTION BNS 75 (Sexual harassment; replaces IPC 354A): (1) A man committing any of the following acts:— (i) physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; or (ii) a demand or request for sexual favours; or (iii) showing pornography against the will of a woman; or (iv) making sexually coloured remarks, shall be guilty of the offence of sexual harassment. (2) Any man who commits the offence specified in clause (i) or clause (ii) or clause (iii) of sub-section (1) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. SECTION BNS 74 (Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty; replaces IPC 354): Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.

material:
SITUATION: Theft, snatching or robbery. The law treats theft, snatching and robbery differently depending on force and where it happened.
STEP 1: If anyone is in danger or injured, call 112.
STEP 2: Write down what was taken, when and where, and anything you remember about the person. Do not confront them.
STEP 3: If a phone, cards or UPI access were taken, call your bank to block cards and UPI and ask your mobile operator to block the SIM. Note the phone's IMEI number from its box or bill.
STEP 4: Report it at a police station. You can give the information at any police station, irrespective of where the offence happened, orally or electronically. [BNSS 173(1)]
STEP 5: Ask for the copy of your information. It must be given to you free of cost. [BNSS 173(2)]
STEP 6: If the police refuse to record it, send the substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate. [BNSS 173(4)]
KEEP READY: Bill, IMEI or serial number of the item; Photos, CCTV locations, witness contacts; Bank and SIM block confirmations; FIR copy
SECTION BNS 303 (Theft; replaces IPC 378, IPC 379): (1) Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person’s consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. Explanation 1.—A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth. Explanation 2.—A moving effected by the same act which affects the severance may be a theft. Explanation 3.—A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which preve
SECTION BNS 305 (Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc; replaces IPC 380): Whoever commits theft— (a) in any building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling or used for the custody of property; or (b) of any means of transport used for the transport of goods or passengers; or (c) of any article or goods from any means of transport used for the transport of goods or passengers; or (d) of idol or icon in any place of worship; or (e) of any property of the Government or of a local authority, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

material:
SITUATION: Police seized your property. Police can seize property connected with an offence, but they must report it and you can apply to get it back.
STEP 1: Ask for the seizure memo (a list of what was taken) and the case or FIR number. Do not sign a list that is wrong.
STEP 2: The officer must report the seizure to the Magistrate. Property can be given to a person on a bond to produce it when required. [BNSS 106(3)]
STEP 3: Apply to the Magistrate for release, with proof that you own it. [BNSS 503]
STEP 4: If the property is already before a court, apply to that court for interim custody. [BNSS 497]
STEP 5: A lawyer can file the release application. Free legal aid: NALSA helpline 15100.
KEEP READY: Seizure memo; Ownership proof: bill, RC, invoice; FIR or case number; ID proof

material:
SITUATION: Cruelty by husband or in-laws, or dowry harassment. Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, including dowry harassment, is a criminal offence. Your safety comes first.
STEP 1: If you are in danger, call 112 or the Women Helpline 181 and go to a safe place such as a relative's home or a shelter.
STEP 2: Keep medical records, photos of injuries, messages, call records and a list of dowry demands and payments.
STEP 3: Report it at any police station. It is written down, read back and signed by you, and you get a copy free of cost. [BNSS 173(1)-(2)]
STEP 4: If the police do not record it, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate. [BNSS 173(4)]
STEP 5: If you and your children are not being supported, a Magistrate can order monthly maintenance. [BNSS 144]
STEP 6: Free legal aid is available from your District Legal Services Authority (NALSA helpline 15100).
KEEP READY: Medical and police records; Messages and recordings; Marriage proof and list of gifts or payments; Contacts of family or neighbours who saw it
OTHER LAWS: Protection orders and the right to stay in the shared home come under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, which is not part of this tool.
SECTION BNS 85 (Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty; replaces IPC 498A): Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
SECTION BNS 86 (Cruelty defined; replaces IPC 498A): For the purposes of section 85, “cruelty” means— (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.
SECTION BNS 115 (Voluntarily causing hurt; replaces IPC 321, IPC 323): (1) Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said “voluntarily to cause hurt”. (2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122 voluntarily causes hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.

material:
SITUATION: Cheating or online fraud. Cheating and fraud can be reported to the police, and for online money fraud speed matters because banks can sometimes freeze the money.
STEP 1: If money left your account, call your bank at once and ask to freeze or reverse the transaction. For online financial fraud also call the national cyber-crime helpline 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in as soon as possible.
STEP 2: If someone calls claiming a relative is in custody, or that you are under 'digital arrest', and asks for money: do not pay. Police never ask for money on a call. Hang up and call the police station or 112 yourself to check.
STEP 3: Do not delete anything. Take screenshots of chats, profiles, payment receipts, transaction IDs, phone numbers and UPI IDs.
STEP 4: Report it to the police. Information can be given by electronic communication. If you do, it is taken on record once you sign it within three days. [BNSS 173(1)]
STEP 5: Ask for a copy of what was recorded. It must be given to you free of cost. [BNSS 173(2)]
STEP 6: If the police refuse, send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, or apply to the Magistrate. [BNSS 173(4)]
KEEP READY: Screenshots and chat exports; Transaction IDs, bank statements; Seller or account details, phone numbers, UPI IDs; Bills and advertisements
OTHER LAWS: Hacking and other online-specific offences are in the IT Act, which is not part of this tool. A pure money dispute with no deception from the start (a loan not repaid, say) may be a civil matter.
